[Textbook misprint: the ionisation enthalpies are printed with the unit "kJ/mol\(^{-1}\)", which reads as kJ\(\cdot\)mol. The unit is kJ mol\(^{-1}\) (equivalently kJ/mol), as Table 7.2 of the chapter is headed. The values themselves are correct.]

S, Cl and Ar are **consecutive members of the same period**. Table 7.1 of the chapter gives their condensed configurations as \(\mathrm{[Ne]3s^23p^4}\), \(\mathrm{[Ne]3s^23p^5}\) and \(\mathrm{[Ne]3s^23p^6}\), so in all three the electron being removed comes from the same (third) shell.

Across a period the nuclear charge rises by one unit at each step while the added electron enters the *same* shell and screens poorly. The effective nuclear charge \(Z_{\text{eff}}\) therefore increases and the atomic radius decreases (S 104 pm, Cl 99 pm). The valence electron is held more and more tightly, so more energy is needed to remove it and the ionisation enthalpy rises:

\(\mathrm{S\ (1000) < Cl\ (1256) < Ar\ (1520)\ kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Argon sits highest for a further reason the chapter gives: it has the completely filled \(\mathrm{ns^2np^6}\) valence shell, an extra-stable closed configuration, so group 18 elements have "very high ionisation energies".

The hydrides of group 16 have the formula \(\mathrm{H_2E}\) and ionise as \(\mathrm{H_2E \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HE^-}\). How readily this happens is governed by the strength of the **H–E bond**.

On going down the group the size of E increases (O 66 pm to Te 137 pm), so the H–E bond lengthens and weakens. Table 7.5 of the chapter gives the bond lengths as 96, 134, 146 and 169 pm and the corresponding bond dissociation enthalpies as 463, 347, 276 and 238 kJ/mol.

A longer, weaker H–E bond releases \(\mathrm{H^+}\) more easily, so the acidic character increases from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\):

\(\mathrm{H_2O < H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te}\)

The measured \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) values in the same table confirm this — 14.0, 7.0, 3.8 and 2.6 — a smaller \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) meaning a stronger acid.

In the laboratory dioxygen is prepared by heating an oxygen-containing salt such as potassium chlorate in the presence of manganese dioxide, which acts as a catalyst:

\(2\mathrm{KClO_3(s)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{MnO_2}]{\text{Heat}} 2\mathrm{KCl(s)} + 3\mathrm{O_2(g)}\)

\(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) lowers the temperature at which the chlorate decomposes; it is not consumed and does not appear in the balanced equation.

Ozone is a powerful oxidising agent because it decomposes readily to liberate nascent oxygen, \(\mathrm{O_3 \longrightarrow O_2 + O}\).

**a. Lead sulfide + ozone.** The sulfide is oxidised to lead sulfate (sulfur going from \(-2\) to \(+6\)):

\(\mathrm{PbS(s)} + 4\mathrm{O_3(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 4\mathrm{O_2(g)}\)

**b. Nitric oxide + ozone.** Nitric oxide is oxidised to nitrogen dioxide:

\(\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_3(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}\)

This second reaction is the one the chapter identifies as the cause of ozone depletion by the nitrogen oxide emitted from car and supersonic-jet exhausts.

Hot, concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises both metals and non-metals, being itself reduced to \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) (sulfur going from \(+6\) to \(+4\)). Two reactions from the chapter:

**1. With a metal (copper):**

\(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\ (\text{conc.}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_4} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Copper is oxidised from 0 to \(+2\).

**2. With a non-metal (carbon):**

\(\mathrm{C} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\ (\text{conc.}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Carbon is oxidised from 0 to \(+4\).

The chapter notes that this oxidising power depends on concentration and temperature: dilute cold \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) behaves like HCl and attacks only metals above hydrogen in the e.m.f. series, whereas the hot concentrated acid also oxidises copper.

Sulfur dioxide, \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), is an **angular (bent) molecule**. The \(\mathrm{O{-}S{-}O}\) bond angle is \(119.5^\circ\), close to the \(120^\circ\) of a trigonal planar arrangement, the deviation being caused by the lone pair on sulfur, which repels the two bond pairs more strongly than they repel each other.

The \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) double bond arises from \(d\pi\!-\!p\pi\) bonding — sideways overlap of a filled \(2p\) orbital of oxygen with an empty \(3d\) orbital of sulfur.

Both sulfur–oxygen bonds are identical in length, because \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) is a **resonance hybrid of two canonical forms** in which the double bond is on one oxygen and then the other:

\(\mathrm{O{=}S{-}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{O{-}S{=}O}\)

Fluorine is restricted to the \(-1\) state for two reasons the chapter gives:

1. **It is the most electronegative element in the periodic table.** It can never be the positively polarised partner in a bond, so it can never be assigned a positive oxidation state.

2. **Its valence shell has no d-orbitals.** Fluorine's configuration is \(\mathrm{[He]2s^22p^5}\); the second shell contains only \(s\) and \(p\) sub-shells, so fluorine cannot expand its octet. It gains or shares one electron, reaching \(-1\), and stops there.

Chlorine, bromine and iodine differ on both counts. They are less electronegative than fluorine, so they can be positively polarised — particularly by fluorine and oxygen — and they have **empty d-orbitals in the valence shell** \((3d, 4d, 5d)\). Their paired valence electrons can be unpaired and promoted into those d-orbitals, allowing them to expand the octet and form one, three, five or seven bonds. Hence they show \(+1\), \(+3\), \(+5\) and \(+7\) in addition to \(-1\), as in \(\mathrm{HOCl}\), \(\mathrm{HClO_2}\), \(\mathrm{HClO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\).

**a. With iron.** Chlorine reacts with metals to form chlorides. With iron it gives ferric chloride, iron being taken to its higher \(+3\) state:

\(2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{FeCl_3}\)

**b. With excess ammonia.** When ammonia is in excess, chlorine gives ammonium chloride and nitrogen:

\(8\mathrm{NH_3}\ (\text{excess}) + 3\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 6\mathrm{NH_4Cl} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

The proportions matter: the chapter notes that with *excess chlorine* instead the product is the explosive nitrogen trichloride, \(\mathrm{NH_3} + 3\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NCl_3} + 3\mathrm{HCl}\).

Hydrogen chloride is prepared in the laboratory by heating sodium chloride (common salt) with concentrated sulfuric acid. The reaction proceeds in two stages:

\(\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \xrightarrow{420\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{NaHSO_4} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

\(\mathrm{NaHSO_4} + \mathrm{NaCl} \xrightarrow{420\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

This works because concentrated sulfuric acid, being far less volatile, displaces the more volatile acid from its salt. The HCl gas evolved is dried by passing it through concentrated sulfuric acid.

The four structures are shown in the accompanying figure (Table 7.13 of the chapter). In each the shape follows from the number of bond pairs and lone pairs on xenon:

1. \(\mathrm{XeF_2}\) — Xe is \(+2\), with 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs. The three lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid and the two fluorines go axial, giving a **linear** molecule.

2. \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\) — Xe is \(+6\), with 6 bond pairs and 1 lone pair. The lone pair distorts the octahedron, giving a **distorted octahedral** shape.

3. \(\mathrm{XeO_3}\) — Xe is \(+6\), with 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair on a tetrahedral framework, giving a **trigonal pyramidal** molecule.

4. \(\mathrm{XeOF_4}\) — Xe is \(+6\), with 5 bond pairs (one oxygen, four fluorines) and 1 lone pair. The lone pair takes one axial position of an octahedron, giving a **square pyramidal** shape with the four fluorines in the base and the oxygen at the apex.

An **interhalogen compound is a neutral compound formed by the combination of atoms of two different halogens**. They arise because although all halogens belong to the same group they differ in electronegativity, so two or more halogen atoms can combine with each other.

The general formula is \(\mathrm{XX'_n}\), where X is the larger, more electropositive halogen (the central atom) and \(\mathrm{X'}\) is the smaller, more electronegative one; the compound is named as the halide of X. A halogen forms an interhalogen only with a halogen of lower electronegativity than itself. Four types exist: \(\mathrm{XX'}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_3}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) and \(\mathrm{XX'_7}\).

**Examples:** \(\mathrm{ClF}\) (chlorine monofluoride) and \(\mathrm{BrF_3}\) (bromine trifluoride).

**a. With ammonia.** Hydrochloric acid reacts with ammonia to give dense white fumes of ammonium chloride:

\(\mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

This is the standard test for either gas.

**b. With sodium carbonate.** *This chapter does not print the reaction of hydrochloric acid with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\).* What it does establish is that HCl is a strong acid \((K_a = 10^7)\). On that basis, being a strong acid it decomposes a carbonate with brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide:

\(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}\)

The carbonic acid first formed is unstable and breaks down into water and carbon dioxide.

**This chapter gives no "Uses" list for hydrogen chloride.** Section 7.11.2 covers only the preparation of HCl, its physical properties and its chemical properties; a uses list is given for chlorine (7.11.1) and for sulfuric acid (7.10.2), but not for HCl. Any list of uses beyond the chapter would be supplied from outside it.

The one application the chapter does state is:

**Preparation of aqua regia.** Mixing three parts of concentrated HCl with one part of concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) gives aqua regia, which dissolves the noble metals gold and platinum:

\(\mathrm{Au} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{NO_3^-} + 4\mathrm{Cl^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{AuCl_4^-} + \mathrm{NO} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

A second point, though the chapter frames it as a property rather than a use, is that HCl gives white fumes of \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\) with ammonia, which is how the gas is identified.

Chlorine forms four oxoacids, one for each of its positive oxidation states. Their structural formulae are shown in the accompanying figure.

| Oxidation state of Cl | Name | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| \(+1\) | Hypochlorous acid | \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) |
| \(+3\) | Chlorous acid | \(\mathrm{HOClO}\) or \(\mathrm{HClO_2}\) |
| \(+5\) | Chloric acid | \(\mathrm{HClO_3}\) |
| \(+7\) | Perchloric acid | \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) |

In every one of them the ionisable hydrogen is attached to oxygen, not to chlorine, and the remaining oxygens are held by \(\mathrm{Cl{=}O}\) double bonds. Only \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) has been isolated in the pure state; the rest are stable only in aqueous solution or as their salts.

The acid strength increases with the oxidation state of chlorine — from \(\mathrm{HOCl}\), a weak acid with \(K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}\), to \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\), a very strong acid with \(K_a \gg 1\).

[Textbook note (not an error): part (a) sets the reaction of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) with \(\mathrm{F_2}\) at 437 K, whereas this chapter's own table of preparations gives \(\mathrm{Cl_2} + \mathrm{F_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{ClF}\) at 523 K in a copper vessel. The product is ClF on either reading; only the stated temperature differs from the chapter.]

**a. Chlorine and fluorine in equal volume.** Direct combination in a 1 : 1 volume ratio gives chlorine monofluoride:

\(\mathrm{Cl_2} + \mathrm{F_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{ClF}\)

ClF is a colourless gas. (The chapter's table of preparations gives this reaction at **523 K in a copper vessel**, not at the 437 K printed in the question.)

**b. Bromine with excess fluorine.** With fluorine in excess bromine is taken to its higher oxidation state, giving bromine trifluoride:

\(\mathrm{Br_2} + 3\mathrm{F_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{BrF_3}\)

\(\mathrm{BrF_3}\) is a yellow-green liquid. This is the only \(\mathrm{Br_2} + \mathrm{F_2}\) equation the chapter prints; it lists \(\mathrm{BrF_5}\) among the \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) compounds but gives no equation for its formation.

Xenon fluorides are prepared by the **direct reaction of xenon with fluorine**, the product depending on the ratio of the two gases and on the conditions (temperature, pressure, electric discharge or photochemical activation):

\(\mathrm{Xe} + \mathrm{F_2} \xrightarrow[\text{Ni tube, } 400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}]{\text{sealed}} \mathrm{XeF_2}\)

\(\mathrm{Xe} + \mathrm{F_2}\ (1 : 5) \xrightarrow[5\text{-}6\ \text{atm}]{\text{Ni tube, } 400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{XeF_4}\)

\(\mathrm{Xe} + 2\mathrm{F_2} \xrightarrow[-80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}]{\text{electric discharge}} \mathrm{XeF_4}\)

\(\mathrm{Xe} + 3\mathrm{F_2} \xrightarrow[\text{low temp.}]{\text{electric discharge}} \mathrm{XeF_6}\)

The more fluorine relative to xenon, the higher the fluoride formed. All three are colourless crystalline solids that sublime readily at 298 K and are powerful fluorinating agents.

**Xenon trioxide, \(\mathrm{XeO_3}\)** — by the hydrolysis of xenon fluorides with water:

\(3\mathrm{XeF_4} + 6\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Xe} + \mathrm{XeO_3} + 12\mathrm{HF} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}\)

\(\mathrm{XeF_6} + 3\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{XeO_3} + 6\mathrm{HF}\)

The first is a disproportionation — some xenon is reduced to the free element and some oxidised to \(\mathrm{XeO_3}\); the second is a straightforward complete hydrolysis.

**Xenon oxytetrafluoride, \(\mathrm{XeOF_4}\)** — by the *partial* hydrolysis of xenon hexafluoride, using only one molecule of water so that only two of the six fluorines are replaced:

\(\mathrm{XeF_6} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{XeOF_4} + 2\mathrm{HF}\)

From Table 7.14 of the chapter.

**Neon** (any two):

1. In neon discharge lamps and signs — these signs are visible from long distances and also in mist or fog.

2. In fluorescent tubes.

(Also: a mixture of Ne and He is used in protective electrical devices such as voltage stabilizers and current rectifiers; and for the production of lasers.)

**Argon** (any two):

1. For producing an inert atmosphere in welding and steel production.

2. A mixture of 85 % Ar and 15 % \(\mathrm{N_2}\) is filled in electric bulbs to increase the life of the filament.

(Also: in filling fluorescent tubes and radio valves; and mixed with neon to give lights of various colours.)

**Structure.** Ozone, \(\mathrm{O_3}\), is an **angular** molecule. Its two \(\mathrm{O{-}O}\) bond lengths are **identical, 128 pm**, and the \(\mathrm{O{-}O{-}O}\) bond angle is about \(117^\circ\). The two bonds are equal because ozone is a **resonance hybrid of two canonical forms**, in which the double bond lies first on one terminal oxygen and then on the other:

\(\mathrm{O{=}O{-}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{O{-}O{=}O}\)

The real molecule is neither form but the hybrid, so each bond is intermediate between a single and a double bond — which is why both measure the same 128 pm. Ozone is **diamagnetic**, having no unpaired electrons.

**Uses** (any two):

1. For air purification at crowded places such as cinema halls, tunnels and railways.

2. In sterilizing drinking water, by oxidising all germs and bacteria.

(Also: for bleaching ivory, oils, starch, wax and delicate fabrics such as silk; and in the manufacture of synthetic camphor and potassium permanganate.)

**i. Atomic radii — increase down the group.** O 66, S 104, Se 117, Te 137, Po 146 pm. On going down the group a new quantum shell is added at each step, so the valence electrons lie further from the nucleus and the atom is larger. The increase in nuclear charge is more than offset by the added shielding.

**ii. Ionisation enthalpy — decreases down the group.** O 1314, S 1000, Se 941, Te 869, Po 813 kJ/mol. As the atom gets larger the valence electron is further from the nucleus and better shielded, so it is held less tightly and less energy is needed to remove it.

**iii. Electronegativity — decreases down the group.** O 3.50, S 2.44, Se 2.48, Te 2.01, Po 1.76. The larger the atom, the weaker its pull on a shared electron pair. Oxygen has the highest electronegativity of the group and, as the chapter notes, the highest of all elements next to fluorine. (Note that the printed value for selenium, 2.48, is marginally *above* that of sulfur, 2.44; the overall fall from 3.50 to 1.76 is the trend being asked about.)

(All values are from Table 7.2 of the chapter.)
